analysis.one_liner: Restores the DEA's power to immediately act against drug companies fueling the opioid epidemic.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to restore the DEA's pre-2016 power to crack down on opioid distributors never got a vote in either subcommittee and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill repeals the 2016 Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act, which raised the bar the Drug Enforcement Administration had to meet before it could deny, suspend, or revoke the federal registration of drug manufacturers, wholesale distributors, and pharmacies that handle controlled substances. Under the 2016 law, the DEA must first give a company notice and a chance to correct problems before acting; before that law, the DEA could act when a registration posed an 'imminent danger' to public health and safety. This bill puts the older, tougher standard back in place and also repeals a related section added by the 2016 law [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families in communities hit by the opioid epidemic, and the DEA itself, which would regain its pre-2016 ability to move immediately against manufacturers, distributors, or pharmacies whose handling of opioid shipments is endangering the public, rather than having to give notice and negotiate first [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Public Law 114-145 (the 2016 Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act), restoring the Controlled Substances Act provisions it had amended so the DEA can deny, revoke, or suspend registrations under the prior standard [S2][S3].

Also repeals section 303(k) of the Controlled Substances Act, a provision the 2016 law added (later redesignated by the 2018 SUPPORT Act), removing the notice-and-compliance framework the 2016 law built into enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers, wholesale distributors, and pharmacies that handle controlled substances would face a faster, easier path to having their DEA registration suspended or revoked, and could lose sales when enforcement interrupts shipments. Some pain patients could face tighter supply if distributors facing scrutiny become more cautious about shipping opioids [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The 2016 law was passed in the name of patient access; its supporters argued that immediate DEA suspensions could cut off legitimate medications to hospitals, pharmacies, and patients, and the notice-and-correct process was meant to prevent that. Restoring the older standard brings back that risk of supply interruptions for lawful users [S2][S3].

Companies facing a registration threat lose a procedural safeguard (advance notice and an opportunity to correct) that was added specifically to protect them from sudden enforcement; critics of repeal view that as a due-process rollback [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the DEA regaining a tool it says it needs to act quickly against companies fueling the opioid epidemic; the cost is less certainty for legitimate handlers of controlled substances and a possible risk of supply disruptions for real patients. Given the death toll of the opioid epidemic, most of the trade-off favors restoration, but the access concerns for pain patients are real and not trivial.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their Health and Crime subcommittees, and neither subcommittee ever took it up; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania, introduced the bill on September 27, 2019, joined by Democratic Representative Ann Kuster of New Hampshire [S1][S3].
Five other House Democrats signed on as cosponsors [S4].

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and within a month both had sent it to subcommittees (Health, and Crime, Terrorism and Homeland Security) [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill and no chamber ever voted on it; the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still sitting at the subcommittee stage [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers and wholesale distributors, who kept the 2016 law's notice-and-correct protections limiting the DEA's ability to quickly suspend or revoke their registrations. Communities affected by the opioid epidemic got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill, the original Democratic coauthor signed on at introduction, and five additional House Democrats cosponsored; no Republican beyond the sponsor appears in the cosponsor list [S4].

industries.note: Repealing the 2016 law removes the notice-and-correct requirement that makes it harder for the DEA to suspend or revoke their registrations, so enforcement could reach them faster and interrupt the supply chains through which opioids reached the street. Their interest in keeping the 2016 law runs directly against communities losing people to overdoses [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Pharmacies and dispensers of controlled substances
industries.note: Dispensers would face the same faster enforcement risk as distributors, but some pharmacies also argue the 2016 law protects them from abrupt supply cutoffs. For patients, the same enforcement could mean either fewer diverted opioids or a harder time filling lawful prescriptions [S2][S3].
